l4_steps.pain_point: KPI thresholds stored in Tableau data sources cannot be version-controlled — rollback after an erroneous threshold change requires DBA intervention to restore a Redshift snapshot, causing 4–8 hours of incorrect reporting

l4_steps.name: Retrieve scheduled work orders for inbound aircraft
l4_steps.input: Published flight schedule and aircraft tail assignment from Amadeus SkyWORKS
l4_steps.output: Work pack listing all due scheduled tasks, AD compliance items, and component changes
l4_steps.kpi: Work pack issued ≥4 hours before estimated aircraft arrival
l4_steps.pain_point: Late schedule changes from network operations can invalidate pre-built work packs; AMOS work order generation requires manual re-trigger when tail swaps occur

l4_steps.name: Load MEL/CDL deferred defect carry-forwards
l4_steps.input: Open defect records from previous station's Electronic Technical Log
l4_steps.output: Annotated work pack with deferred items, MEL interval expiry dates, and required rectification actions
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of Category B/C MEL items captured before aircraft arrival; zero Category A items carried forward
l4_steps.pain_point: ETL records from outstations transmitted via ACARS can arrive incomplete; discrepancies between paper ATL and AMOS electronic record create compliance exposure

l4_steps.name: Confirm parts, tools, and crew availability
l4_steps.input: Work pack task list and station inventory snapshot from AMOS stores module
l4_steps.output: Resource-confirmed work pack or escalation to AOG desk for missing items
l4_steps.kpi: Resource confirmation completed ≥2 hours before arrival; parts availability ≥95% for scheduled tasks
l4_steps.pain_point: Station stock levels for consumables (O-rings, filters, fluids) are often below safety stock due to demand spikes; AMOS min/max reorder logic not consistently tuned per station size

l4_steps.name: Receive Electronic Technical Log from flight crew
l4_steps.input: Completed ETL entries from captain (defects, oil uptakes, cabin reports) transmitted via FliteDeck EFB
l4_steps.output: Acknowledged defect list with timestamp of handover; open items transferred to AMOS
l4_steps.kpi: ETL handover completed within 10 minutes of blocks-on; 100% of defects transferred to AMOS within 15 minutes
l4_steps.pain_point: EFB-to-MRO system integration gaps require manual re-keying of defects into AMOS at some stations, introducing transcription risk and adding 10–15 minutes to turnaround

l4_steps.name: Categorise open defects by MEL interval and severity
l4_steps.input: Defect entries from ETL handover; MEL/MMEL reference document in AMOS
l4_steps.output: Prioritised defect list: Category A (immediate), B (3 days), C (10 days), D (120 days)
l4_steps.kpi: Defect categorisation completed within 5 minutes of ETL receipt; zero mis-categorisations identified at next audit
l4_steps.pain_point: Engineers at outstations may lack current AMM/MEL revision; AMOS does not auto-flag MEL revision mismatches between aircraft effectivity and loaded document version

l4_steps.name: Assess Category A defects and trigger AOG response
l4_steps.input: Categorised defect list; FAR Part 43 and airline MOE airworthiness standards
l4_steps.output: AOG work order raised in AMOS with resource and parts requirements; MCC notified via ACARS/phone bridge
l4_steps.kpi: AOG notification to MCC within 5 minutes of Category A identification; AOG rectification plan confirmed within 30 minutes
l4_steps.pain_point: MCC visibility of real-time station technician availability is limited; AOG coordination relies on phone bridge rather than integrated workforce management, causing delays during high-disruption events

l4_steps.name: Perform exterior walkaround inspection per AMM 05-10
l4_steps.input: Approved work pack with transit check task cards; AMM Chapter 05-10 inspection criteria
l4_steps.output: Signed-off walkaround task card in AMOS; new defects raised as open items
l4_steps.kpi: Walkaround completed within 15 minutes of blocks-on; defect detection rate benchmarked against fleet average
l4_steps.pain_point: Short turnaround windows (25–45 min at focus cities) compress walkaround time; pressure to dispatch on-time can lead to incomplete checks — a known FAA audit finding category

l4_steps.name: Service aircraft fluids — fuel, engine oil, hydraulic, LOX
l4_steps.input: Fuel uplift order from flight dispatch (Jeppesen FliteDeck); oil consumption trend from CAMP
l4_steps.output: Fluid servicing task cards signed off; uplift quantities logged in AMOS and transmitted to fuel vendor
l4_steps.kpi: Engine oil consumption ≤0.3 qt/hr per engine; hydraulic fluid level within limits; LOX quantity per MEL minimum
l4_steps.pain_point: High oil consumption trending on CFM56-7B engines requires tracking against CAMP trend monitoring; deferred oil top-ups due to short turns inflate consumption variance and can trigger premature engine shop visit

l4_steps.name: Complete avionics and safety equipment functional checks
l4_steps.input: Transit check task card list; crew defect reports referencing avionics squawks
l4_steps.output: Signed-off avionics check records; unresolved items escalated to LAME for MEL assessment
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of safety-critical checks (fire detection, ELT, emergency lighting) signed off before departure; zero open avionics items departing without MEL disposition
l4_steps.pain_point: Some avionics functional checks require aircraft power-up with full flight deck crew, creating coordination bottleneck during short turns; no automated power-on sequencing tool integrated with AMOS task card sign-off

l4_steps.name: Verify all turnaround check items signed off
l4_steps.input: Task card completion status from AMT team; turnaround clock from Amadeus Airport Management System
l4_steps.output: Check completion record in AMOS; ground time extension request if items outstanding
l4_steps.kpi: All transit check items signed off ≥10 minutes before scheduled departure; ground time extension rate <5% of transits
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS task card sign-off visibility is station-level only; MCC cannot see real-time completion percentage across all active turns without custom Tableau dashboard — gap identified in 2024 operational review

l4_steps.name: Diagnose defect per AMM/TSM fault isolation procedures
l4_steps.input: Open defect record from ETL; AMM and TSM fault isolation chapters accessed via AMOS document portal
l4_steps.output: Confirmed root cause; work scope defined; parts demand raised in AMOS
l4_steps.kpi: Fault isolation completed within 30 minutes for 80% of line defects; correct-fix-first-time rate ≥92%
l4_steps.pain_point: TSM procedures for avionics LRUs require BITE readout from centralised maintenance computer, which is unavailable to AMTs without Airbus/Boeing tooling licences at some outstations

l4_steps.name: Check station stock and raise parts demand in AMOS
l4_steps.input: Confirmed parts requirement from LAME; AMOS station inventory snapshot
l4_steps.output: Parts issued from stock or AOG purchase order raised; estimated delivery time confirmed
l4_steps.kpi: Parts issued within 20 minutes for in-stock items; AOG order placed within 15 minutes of stock-out confirmation
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS inventory sync with SAP S/4HANA Finance for parts valuation runs on 4-hour batch cycle; real-time availability data not always reflected, leading to manual phone confirmation with stores

l4_steps.name: Apply MEL deferral if part unavailable within turn
l4_steps.input: MEL/MMEL reference; confirmed parts ETA vs. departure time; defect record in AMOS
l4_steps.output: MEL deferral entry in CAMP airworthiness tracking; placard installed on aircraft; copy transmitted to MCC
l4_steps.kpi: MEL deferral completed and documented within 20 minutes of stock-out decision; deferred defect interval compliance 100% at next station
l4_steps.pain_point: CAMP airworthiness record and AMOS open defect record are maintained in parallel without bidirectional sync; duplicate data entry risk creates interval tracking errors identified in FAA surveillance programmes

l4_steps.name: Verify rectification completed before departure
l4_steps.input: LAME sign-off notification from AMOS; departure countdown from Amadeus Airport Management System
l4_steps.output: Rectification confirmed closed in AMOS or deferred via MEL; gate hold issued to operations if incomplete
l4_steps.kpi: Rectification confirmed ≥15 minutes before scheduled departure for 90% of defects; gate hold rate due to maintenance <2% of departures
l4_steps.pain_point: MCC must coordinate between AMOS (maintenance status) and Amadeus AMS (gate/departure status) via manual phone bridge; no unified operations dashboard causes coordination lag during peak disruption periods

l4_steps.name: Perform final inspection and duplicate check if required
l4_steps.input: Completed task cards and rectification records; regulatory requirement for duplicate inspection (CAR 43 / EASA Part-145)
l4_steps.output: Final inspection sign-off in AMOS; duplicate inspection record if flight control or engine reassembly performed
l4_steps.kpi: Duplicate inspection rate 100% for required work scopes; zero departures with open duplicate inspection requirement
l4_steps.pain_point: Identifying which tasks legally require duplicate independent inspection is not automated in AMOS task card setup; relies on engineer knowledge and MOE references, creating inconsistency across station experience levels

l4_steps.name: Issue Certificate of Release to Service in AMOS
l4_steps.input: All task cards signed off; no outstanding Category A defects; completed final inspection record
l4_steps.output: CRS/RTS issued in AMOS with LAME licence number, authorisation scope, and timestamp; aircraft released to operations
l4_steps.kpi: CRS issued ≥10 minutes before scheduled departure; 100% of CRS entries include mandatory regulatory fields per Part-145/FAR 43
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS CRS module requires manual licence validity check; no real-time integration with national aviation authority (NAA) licence database means expired or scope-exceeded authorisations are only caught during audits

l4_steps.name: Update Electronic Technical Log and close open items
l4_steps.input: CRS issued in AMOS; rectification and deferral records
l4_steps.output: ETL updated with all maintenance actions, deferred items, and CRS reference; clean ATL handed to flight crew
l4_steps.kpi: ETL closed within 5 minutes of CRS; zero discrepancies between AMOS work order record and ETL at post-flight audit
l4_steps.pain_point: FliteDeck ETL and AMOS work order closure are separate manual entries with no automated reconciliation; discrepancies create compliance findings during IOSA audits and require costly manual reconciliation

l4_steps.name: Close all work orders and task cards in AMOS
l4_steps.input: LAME sign-off notifications; CRS reference number
l4_steps.output: All work orders closed with actual man-hours, materials consumed, and defect codes recorded
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of work orders closed within 2 hours of aircraft departure; man-hour variance vs. estimate ≤15%
l4_steps.pain_point: Actual man-hour capture at line stations is often done retrospectively and inaccurately; affects MRO cost modelling and future work scope estimates in AMOS planning module

l4_steps.name: Log component removals and installations in CAMP
l4_steps.input: Parts demand fulfilment records from AMOS; component serial and part numbers
l4_steps.output: Airworthiness record updated in CAMP with installation dates, cycles, and time-since-new for tracked components
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of life-limited parts (LLPs) and hard-time components logged within 4 hours of installation; zero untracked LLP removals per CAMP audit
l4_steps.pain_point: Manual entry of component records into CAMP is error-prone at outstations; LLP tracking errors can result in components exceeding overhaul limits — a direct airworthiness risk with significant FAA fine exposure

l4_steps.name: Transmit maintenance data to central MRO analytics platform
l4_steps.input: Closed work orders, defect codes, man-hours, and component records from AMOS and CAMP
l4_steps.output: Maintenance event dataset available in AWS Redshift for reliability analysis, cost tracking, and Tableau dashboards
l4_steps.kpi: Data transmission latency <30 minutes post work order closure; data completeness score ≥98% per monthly reliability report
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS-to-AWS data pipeline relies on scheduled batch exports rather than real-time streaming; 4–6 hour data lag means MCC reliability dashboards do not reflect same-day defect trends during disruption events

l4_steps.name: Extract aircraft maintenance due-date forecast
l4_steps.input: Aircraft flight hours, cycles, and calendar days from ACARS/flight ops feeds
l4_steps.output: Due-date forecast report showing C/D check windows per tail number
l4_steps.kpi: Forecast horizon ≥12 months; 100% of fleet tails covered
l4_steps.pain_point: CAMP data sync lag from ACARS can understate actual FH/FC by 1-2 cycles, risking check due-date miscalculation

l4_steps.name: Review AD/SB compliance status per tail
l4_steps.input: FAA Airworthiness Directives feed, manufacturer Service Bulletins, CAMP compliance tracker
l4_steps.output: AD/SB compliance gap list with mandated incorporation deadlines
l4_steps.kpi: Zero open mandatory ADs at check induction; SB review complete ≥90 days pre-induction
l4_steps.pain_point: Rapid-fire AD releases (e.g. Boeing MAX ADs post-737 MAX groundings) can invalidate a pre-built work scope days before induction

l4_steps.name: Determine check type: C-check vs D-check
l4_steps.input: Aircraft age, total flight cycles, last heavy check date, AD requirements
l4_steps.output: Confirmed check type decision (C1/C2/C3 or D-check) entered in AMOS
l4_steps.kpi: Check type confirmed ≥9 months prior to induction date
l4_steps.pain_point: Legacy aircraft approaching D-check thresholds (typically 8-12 years) may be upgraded mid-plan; late D-check designation inflates TAT and cost >40%

l4_steps.name: Generate MPD baseline work package in AMOS
l4_steps.input: Approved check type, aircraft MPD (Boeing Maintenance Planning Document), AMOS task library
l4_steps.output: Baseline work package with task cards, intervals, and estimated manhours
l4_steps.kpi: Baseline work package issued ≥8 months prior to induction; manhour estimate accuracy ±10%
l4_steps.pain_point: MPD revision cycles from Boeing (quarterly) can introduce new tasks after baseline is locked, requiring rework of the work package

l4_steps.name: Incorporate deferred defects and open MEL items
l4_steps.input: Deferred defect register, MEL (Minimum Equipment List) open items from line maintenance logs
l4_steps.output: Updated work package with deferred items assigned to check package
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of Category A/B MEL items resolved at or before heavy check; deferred defect backlog cleared
l4_steps.pain_point: MEL items deferred beyond permissible intervals can trigger unplanned component removals, extending TAT by 3-5 days

l4_steps.name: Add Engineering Orders and requested modifications
l4_steps.input: Engineering Orders (EOs), STC modifications, cabin reconfiguration requests from fleet planning
l4_steps.output: Supplemental work scope with EOs and mods task-carded in AMOS
l4_steps.kpi: All approved EOs incorporated ≥6 months pre-induction; no scope additions within 60 days of induction
l4_steps.pain_point: Cabin modification requests (seat layout changes, IFE upgrades) arriving late can increase ground time by 5-10 days and require renegotiation of MRO slot

l4_steps.name: Validate work scope against C-check threshold
l4_steps.input: Completed work scope package, manhour estimates, EO add-ons
l4_steps.output: Scope classification confirmed: C-check or escalated to D-check in AMOS
l4_steps.kpi: Scope re-classification decisions completed within 5 business days of scope freeze; re-scope rate <5% of planned checks
l4_steps.pain_point: Scope creep during D-check escalation is poorly controlled — cumulative EOs can push TAT from 21 days to 45 days without formal gate review

l4_steps.name: Estimate total manhours and skill requirements
l4_steps.input: Approved work scope package with task cards
l4_steps.output: Manhour demand plan broken down by trade (structures, avionics, engines, interiors)
l4_steps.kpi: Manhour forecast accuracy ±15% vs actuals; plan issued ≥6 months pre-induction
l4_steps.pain_point: Structures trade skill shortages at third-party MROs (particularly composite repair) can stretch avail windows; market-rate labour cost escalation unpredictable >6 months out

l4_steps.name: Identify and order long-lead rotable parts
l4_steps.input: AMOS work package BOM, CAMP part cross-reference, current inventory positions
l4_steps.output: Long-lead parts list with order quantities, lead times, and due-in dates
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of long-lead parts (lead time >90 days) on order ≥6 months pre-induction; stockout rate at induction <2%
l4_steps.pain_point: Boeing 737 MAX supply chain disruptions (e.g. Spirit AeroSystems fuselage quality holds 2024) can delay rotable availability by 4-8 weeks, forcing work scope deferral

l4_steps.name: Raise material requisitions for consumables and hardware
l4_steps.input: AMOS-generated materials list, approved vendor catalogue in SAP Ariba
l4_steps.output: Purchase requisitions raised and approved in SAP Ariba; delivery schedule confirmed
l4_steps.kpi: All consumable PRs raised ≥90 days pre-induction; on-time delivery rate ≥95%
l4_steps.pain_point: Spot-buy requirements for unplanned findings inflate procurement cost by 20-40%; Ariba spot-buy approvals can take 5-10 days, delaying line opening

l4_steps.name: Confirm critical parts availability at MRO site
l4_steps.input: SAP Ariba purchase orders, MRO facility inventory feed, Boeing Toolbox part status
l4_steps.output: Parts readiness confirmation report; open shortages escalated
l4_steps.kpi: Parts readiness confirmation completed 30 days pre-induction; critical shortage count = 0 at induction
l4_steps.pain_point: MRO-to-airline inventory visibility gaps mean shortages are discovered at induction rather than pre-induction, causing AOG-equivalent delays mid-check

l4_steps.name: Issue RFQ to approved heavy MRO facilities
l4_steps.input: Approved work scope package, manhour estimates, parts supply plan, desired induction window
l4_steps.output: RFQ document issued to ≥3 qualified MRO vendors via SAP Ariba sourcing event
l4_steps.kpi: RFQ issued ≥9 months pre-induction; minimum 3 qualified vendor responses received
l4_steps.pain_point: Global MRO capacity constraints (post-pandemic backlog) reduce competitive vendor responses; sole-source situations remove cost leverage and inflate quotes by 15-30%

l4_steps.name: Evaluate vendor bids on TAT, cost, and capability
l4_steps.input: Vendor bids, MRO capability audit records, historical TAT performance data
l4_steps.output: Bid evaluation scorecard with vendor ranking; recommendation memo
l4_steps.kpi: Evaluation complete within 15 business days of bid close; cost variance between lowest and selected bid <8%
l4_steps.pain_point: MRO vendors routinely under-quote TAT to win contract then invoke 'findings escalation' clauses — actual TAT can exceed quoted by 20-35%, disrupting aircraft utilisation plan

l4_steps.name: Confirm bid meets TAT and unit cost targets
l4_steps.input: Bid evaluation scorecard, fleet plan TAT requirements, approved MRO budget
l4_steps.output: Approved vendor selection or instruction to re-issue RFQ / negotiate
l4_steps.kpi: Contract TAT ≤21 days for C-check, ≤45 days for D-check; unit cost within ±5% of approved budget
l4_steps.pain_point: Approval delays at VP level (budget cycles, contract committee scheduling) can compress negotiation window, forcing acceptance of sub-optimal bids

l4_steps.name: Award contract and raise PO in SAP
l4_steps.input: Approved vendor selection, agreed contract terms, budget approval
l4_steps.output: Signed MRO contract, purchase order raised in SAP S/4HANA, cost centre committed
l4_steps.kpi: PO raised within 5 business days of approval; contract signed ≥6 months pre-induction
l4_steps.pain_point: SAP Ariba–to–S/4HANA PO hand-off failures (integration errors) can delay cost commitment, blocking parts release and hangar slot confirmation

l4_steps.name: Compile aircraft technical documentation package
l4_steps.input: Aircraft log books, CAMP airworthiness records, work scope package, AD/SB status report
l4_steps.output: Complete pre-induction documentation pack transmitted to MRO facility
l4_steps.kpi: Documentation package delivered to MRO ≥14 days before induction; zero missing mandatory documents at induction gate
l4_steps.pain_point: Paper-based or siloed digital records from legacy line maintenance systems create gaps in technical records; missing logbook entries can halt induction pending FAA review

l4_steps.name: Coordinate ferry flight and fleet schedule impact
l4_steps.input: Confirmed MRO induction date, aircraft tail assignment, fleet plan from SkyWORKS
l4_steps.output: Ferry flight plan, substitute aircraft allocation, schedule change notification to OCC
l4_steps.kpi: Ferry flight confirmed ≥21 days pre-induction; schedule impact to revenue flying <2 affected rotations
l4_steps.pain_point: Last-minute fleet reassignments to cover operational disruptions can pull the designated heavy-check aircraft back into service, delaying induction and incurring MRO slot-break fees

l4_steps.name: Complete pre-induction readiness checklist
l4_steps.input: Documentation pack status, parts delivery confirmations, ferry flight plan, MRO slot confirmation
l4_steps.output: Signed pre-induction checklist; go/no-go decision for induction
l4_steps.kpi: Checklist signed-off 7 days pre-induction; no-go rate due to planning gaps <3%
l4_steps.pain_point: No-go decisions within 7 days of induction trigger MRO penalty fees (typically $15-25K/day for slot breaks) and ripple delay to subsequent planned checks

l4_steps.name: Receive engine from aircraft and log induction
l4_steps.input: Engine removal notification from line maintenance or heavy check
l4_steps.output: Engine induction record with serial number, TSN, CSN, and removal reason
l4_steps.kpi: Induction record created within 4 hours of engine receipt
l4_steps.pain_point: Incomplete removal documentation from line stations delays accurate TSN/CSN capture, risking life-limit tracking errors in AMOS

l4_steps.name: Perform incoming borescope inspection of engine
l4_steps.input: Induction record, engine removal reason, last borescope findings
l4_steps.output: Borescope inspection report with blade condition, FOD, and erosion findings
l4_steps.kpi: Borescope inspection completed within 24 hours of induction; findings logged in AMOS within 2 hours of inspection
l4_steps.pain_point: FOD damage discovered at induction not captured in aircraft logbook leads to retroactive safety investigations under FAR Part 43.9 and delays work scope confirmation

l4_steps.name: Determine shop visit type and open work order
l4_steps.input: Borescope report, engine removal reason, performance trend data
l4_steps.output: Shop visit classification (Performance Restoration, HSI, or On-Condition) and AMOS work order
l4_steps.kpi: Work order opened and shop visit type confirmed within 8 hours of induction
l4_steps.pain_point: Performance trend data from on-wing ACARS monitoring (SITA ACARS) may not sync to AMOS automatically, forcing manual EGT margin entry and introducing transcription errors

l4_steps.name: Disassemble engine modules per CMM procedures
l4_steps.input: AMOS work order, OEM Component Maintenance Manual (CMM), tooling list
l4_steps.output: Disassembled engine modules staged for inspection; AMOS task cards signed off
l4_steps.kpi: Module teardown completed within published CMM man-hour estimate ±10%
l4_steps.pain_point: OEM CMM revision cycle (Boeing/CFM/GE) lags regulatory changes; AMOS document revision alerts can be suppressed by users, risking use of superseded procedures

l4_steps.name: Inspect HPC, HPT, LPT, and fan modules
l4_steps.input: Disassembled modules, OEM Airworthiness Limitations (AWL), AD compliance matrix
l4_steps.output: Module inspection findings report; life-limited part (LLP) status updated in AMOS
l4_steps.kpi: 100% LLP cycle verification against AMOS life-limit records; inspection findings report issued within 48 hours of module receipt
l4_steps.pain_point: LLP cycle counter discrepancies between AMOS and Boeing Toolbox / CAMP cause certification holds; reconciliation requires manual cross-check, averaging 6–8 hours per engine

l4_steps.name: Identify AD/SB compliance gaps and raise EOs
l4_steps.input: Module inspection report, FAA AD database, OEM service bulletin index
l4_steps.output: Engineering Orders (EOs) raised in AMOS for each open AD/SB; updated work scope
l4_steps.kpi: Zero open mandatory ADs at engine release; all applicable SBs evaluated within 24 hours of findings report
l4_steps.pain_point: FAA AD compliance is checked against AMOS AD library which requires manual updates; a delayed AD import (>30 days) creates regulatory exposure under FAR Part 91.409 and Part 43 Appendix D

l4_steps.name: Classify parts as BER, serviceable, or repairable
l4_steps.input: Teardown findings report, OEM serviceability limits, repair cost benchmarks
l4_steps.output: Parts disposition list with BER (Beyond Economic Repair), serviceable, and repair-route tags in AMOS
l4_steps.kpi: Parts disposition completed within 48 hours of teardown; BER rate benchmarked at ≤15% of total parts count
l4_steps.pain_point: BER decisions without OEM-approved repair data require Designated Engineering Representative (DER) approval under FAR Part 145.109, adding 3–10 days per non-standard repair route

l4_steps.name: Check rotable parts availability in pool
l4_steps.input: Parts disposition list, rotable pool inventory records
l4_steps.output: Availability confirmation or shortage list for critical engine parts
l4_steps.kpi: Rotable pool fill rate ≥85% for engine shop demand; critical part shortage identified within 4 hours of disposition
l4_steps.pain_point: CAMP and AMOS rotable inventory records are not always real-time synced; double-allocation of serviceable parts across concurrent shop visits causes last-minute shortages and AOG escalations

l4_steps.name: Raise purchase orders for parts shortages
l4_steps.input: Shortage list from CAMP, approved vendor list (AVL), engine TAT deadline
l4_steps.output: SAP Ariba purchase orders for parts; expected delivery dates entered in AMOS parts tracking
l4_steps.kpi: PO raised within 8 hours of shortage confirmation; expedited orders for AOG parts placed within 2 hours
l4_steps.pain_point: SAP Ariba approved vendor list (AVL) may not include all OEM-authorised repair vendors; purchasing outside AVL requires Finance exception approval adding 24–48 hours to critical-path parts

l4_steps.name: Repair and overhaul modules per CMM
l4_steps.input: Module inspection report, EOs, CMM repair procedures, serviceable replacement parts
l4_steps.output: Repaired modules with AMOS task cards signed; NDT records attached
l4_steps.kpi: Repair man-hours within ±15% of AMOS work-order estimate; first-pass quality rate ≥92%
l4_steps.pain_point: Specialised repair capabilities (e.g., HPT blade tip restore, HPC coating) often require sub-vendor routing; each external repair adds 7–21 days TAT and requires dual-release documentation under EASA Part 145.A.75

l4_steps.name: Apply approved modifications and service bulletins
l4_steps.input: Open SB list from Step 2.3, OEM modification kits, Engineering Orders
l4_steps.output: Modification compliance records in AMOS; updated engine configuration baseline
l4_steps.kpi: 100% mandatory SB incorporation confirmed before assembly; optional SB cost/benefit review completed within 4 hours
l4_steps.pain_point: OEM modification kit availability is frequently constrained (CFM LEAP kits lead times 90–180 days); planning teams must lock SB scope 6+ months before shop visit to avoid TAT overruns

l4_steps.name: Reassemble engine and verify build standard
l4_steps.input: Repaired and serviceable modules, torque specifications, build standard document
l4_steps.output: Fully assembled engine; AMOS build record with component serial numbers and final configuration
l4_steps.kpi: Assembly completed within 48 hours of all parts arrival; dimensional check non-conformance rate ≤5%
l4_steps.pain_point: Configuration mismatch between AMOS build record and physical engine (e.g., wrong fan blade set) is not caught until test cell, costing 12–24 hours of re-teardown time

l4_steps.name: Install engine on test cell and configure parameters
l4_steps.input: Assembled engine, test cell acceptance test procedure (ATP), engine spec sheet
l4_steps.output: Engine installed on test cell; baseline parameters configured in Trax test run record
l4_steps.kpi: Test cell installation completed within 4 hours; test cell utilisation rate ≥80%
l4_steps.pain_point: Test cell scheduling conflicts between engine shop and contracted MRO customers reduce throughput; dynamic slot allocation is managed manually via spreadsheet, not integrated with AMOS shop scheduling

l4_steps.name: Run engine acceptance test per ECTM limits
l4_steps.input: OEM Acceptance Test Procedure (ATP), Engine Condition Trend Monitoring (ECTM) limits, test cell instrumentation data
l4_steps.output: Test run data report: EGT margin, fuel flow, vibration, oil consumption vs. OEM limits
l4_steps.kpi: EGT margin ≥25°C at end-of-test; vibration ≤0.5 in/sec; oil consumption ≤0.5 qt/hr
l4_steps.pain_point: ECTM limits defined in Trax must match the engine variant spec sheet; configuration mismatch between test cell software version and OEM ATP revision causes out-of-tolerance alerts that require manual waiver processing

l4_steps.name: Complete FAA 8130-3 / EASA Form 1 release docs
l4_steps.input: Test cell certification, AMOS work order completion data, AD/SB compliance records
l4_steps.output: FAA 8130-3 or EASA Form 1 Authorised Release Certificate; closed AMOS work order
l4_steps.kpi: Release documentation completed within 8 hours of test cell sign-off; zero documentation deficiencies at FAA/EASA audit
l4_steps.pain_point: Dual-release requirements (FAA 8130-3 and EASA Form 1) for engines operated on international routes require two signatories with current authorisations; signatory availability is a recurring bottleneck, especially on night shifts

l4_steps.name: Update engine life history and rotable records
l4_steps.input: Closed AMOS work order, LLP cycle updates, modification compliance records
l4_steps.output: Updated engine life history in CAMP; rotable pool inventory record updated with new TSO/CSO
l4_steps.kpi: Engine history updated within 4 hours of work order closure; LLP discrepancy rate ≤0.1% at next audit
l4_steps.pain_point: CAMP and AMOS are not bidirectionally integrated in all configurations; manual re-entry of cycle counts from AMOS into CAMP introduces transcription errors that create airworthiness record discrepancies requiring DFP investigation

l4_steps.name: Obtain QA airworthiness release approval
l4_steps.input: Complete AMOS work order, release certificate, CAMP history update confirmation
l4_steps.output: QA-signed airworthiness release; engine cleared for return to rotable pool or direct fitment
l4_steps.kpi: QA release granted within 4 hours of documentation package submission; zero engines released with open corrective actions
l4_steps.pain_point: QA holds caused by incomplete corrective action evidence in AMOS (e.g., missing NDT report attachments) are the leading cause of engine release delays, averaging 6–12 hours per incident

l4_steps.name: Return engine to rotable pool and notify planning
l4_steps.input: QA airworthiness release, engine storage requirements, fleet demand forecast
l4_steps.output: Engine tagged serviceable in AMOS rotable pool; network planning team notified of availability
l4_steps.kpi: Engine available in rotable pool within 2 hours of QA release; total shop visit TAT vs. target reported monthly
l4_steps.pain_point: Rotable pool engine availability is not directly visible in SkyWORKS fleet assignment planning; network and maintenance planning teams rely on manual notifications, creating misalignment between engine availability and scheduled aircraft return-to-service dates

l4_steps.name: Generate parts demand forecast from maintenance programme
l4_steps.input: Approved maintenance programme, fleet utilisation plan, AD/SB list
l4_steps.output: 12-month rolling parts demand forecast by P/N
l4_steps.kpi: Forecast accuracy ≥85% (MAPE ≤15%)
l4_steps.pain_point: Fleet mix changes (737 MAX vs 737-800 intermix) cause demand volatility; AMOS forecast module requires manual adjustment for new-type introductions where consumption history is sparse

l4_steps.name: Validate forecast against consumption history and ADs
l4_steps.input: 24-month parts consumption history, current AD/SB revision delta
l4_steps.output: Validated demand plan with confidence bands; exception list for manual override
l4_steps.kpi: Forecast review cycle completed within 5 business days
l4_steps.pain_point: Sporadic demand items (rotables with <4 removals/year) produce unreliable AMOS statistical forecasts; manual override requires SME judgement and is not auditable within AMOS

l4_steps.name: Submit demand plan to procurement and finance for budget approval
l4_steps.input: Validated demand plan, prior-year actuals
l4_steps.output: Approved materials budget, MRP requirements released to procurement
l4_steps.kpi: Budget approval lead time ≤10 business days
l4_steps.pain_point: No native AMOS–SAP interface at many carriers; demand plan must be manually re-keyed into SAP MRP, introducing transcription errors and plan drift between systems

l4_steps.name: Check stock availability against net demand requirements
l4_steps.input: Approved demand plan, real-time inventory snapshot
l4_steps.output: Net requirements list with buy / borrow / exchange decisions per P/N
l4_steps.kpi: Stock-out rate ≤2% for critical AOG-flagged parts
l4_steps.pain_point: Inventory accuracy degrades when technicians issue parts without closing work orders in AMOS; phantom stock causes missed AOG events and emergency buys that erode savings from planned procurement

l4_steps.name: Source parts from approved vendor list via RFQ
l4_steps.input: Net requirements list, approved vendor master, contract pricing
l4_steps.output: RFQ issued to ≥2 approved suppliers per part number
l4_steps.kpi: Vendor lead time compliance ≥90%; RFQ issued within 1 business day of requirement
l4_steps.pain_point: FAA/EASA Part 145 approved supplier list is slow to update; unapproved parts risk is highest on spot-market buys where non-qualified vendors are used to satisfy urgent demand

l4_steps.name: Evaluate supplier quotes and select preferred source
l4_steps.input: Supplier quotes, cost and lead-time matrix, AOG flag
l4_steps.output: Awarded PO, supplier selection rationale documented
l4_steps.kpi: PO cycle time ≤3 business days (AOG: ≤4 hours)
l4_steps.pain_point: AOG situations force bypass of normal sourcing controls; expedited buys from non-preferred vendors increase counterfeit-part risk and undermine FAR Part 145 traceability requirements

l4_steps.name: Issue purchase order and confirm supplier delivery commitment
l4_steps.input: Awarded quote, budget confirmation, delivery address
l4_steps.output: PO issued with confirmed expected receipt date and freight tracking reference
l4_steps.kpi: PO-to-delivery on-time rate ≥88%
l4_steps.pain_point: International freight delays for OEM parts (Boeing, CFM International); post-2022 supply chain disruption continues to affect lead times for 737 MAX-specific components, inflating AOG exposure

l4_steps.name: Receive parts shipment and verify airworthiness documentation
l4_steps.input: Inbound shipment, packing list, FAA 8130-3 or EASA Form 1
l4_steps.output: Goods receipt logged in AMOS; documents scanned and attached to part record
l4_steps.kpi: Receiving processing time ≤4 hours for AOG-flagged parts; ≤24 hours for routine receipts
l4_steps.pain_point: Incomplete or missing FAA 8130-3 / EASA Form 1 is common on spot-market purchases; quarantine and supplier chase delays average 3–5 days, directly extending AOG events

l4_steps.name: Inspect parts for airworthiness and serviceable condition
l4_steps.input: Physical part, airworthiness release certificate, inspection checklist
l4_steps.output: Inspection record; pass/fail determination recorded against part in AMOS
l4_steps.kpi: Inspection turn-time ≤8 hours; incoming rejection rate ≤3%
l4_steps.pain_point: Counterfeit parts detection requires detailed visual and dimensional checks; AMOS quality module lacks integration with industry counterfeit databases (IATA TACT, EASA SACA) forcing manual cross-reference

l4_steps.name: Quarantine non-conforming parts and raise supplier NCR
l4_steps.input: Failed inspection record, non-conformance details
l4_steps.output: Quarantine tag applied, Non-Conformance Report raised, supplier notified
l4_steps.kpi: NCR resolution cycle ≤15 business days; quarantined parts segregated within 1 hour of rejection
l4_steps.pain_point: Quarantine storage space is constrained at line stations; disposal of life-limited parts requires documented destruction to prevent re-entry into supply chain per FAA Order 8120.11

l4_steps.name: Assign bin location and update AMOS inventory record
l4_steps.input: Accepted and inspected part, warehouse bin map
l4_steps.output: Part binned, inventory record updated with location, quantity, and batch traceability
l4_steps.kpi: Inventory location accuracy ≥99.5%; bin assignment completed within 2 hours of acceptance
l4_steps.pain_point: Barcode label degradation in hangar environments (heat, hydraulic fluid) causes scan failures and phantom inventory; manual overrides bypass AMOS audit trail, creating traceability gaps

l4_steps.name: Monitor shelf-life, expiry dates, and life-limited part counters
l4_steps.input: Part life data, calendar expiry dates, flight-cycle counters from OEM CMM
l4_steps.output: Expiry alerts actioned; scrapping orders raised for time-expired or cycle-expired parts
l4_steps.kpi: Shelf-life compliance 100%; zero expired parts issued from serviceable stock
l4_steps.pain_point: Elastomeric seals and composite consumables have 12–24 month shelf lives; AMOS expiry alerts require manual acknowledgement — risk of expired parts being issued if alert is dismissed without action

l4_steps.name: Conduct periodic cycle counts and reconcile inventory discrepancies
l4_steps.input: Cycle count schedule, physical count results, AMOS on-hand quantities
l4_steps.output: Reconciled inventory record; adjustment or write-off requests submitted to Finance
l4_steps.kpi: Inventory accuracy post-count ≥99%; cycle count variance ≤1% by value
l4_steps.pain_point: High-velocity consumables (O-rings, safety wire, lockwire) are difficult to count accurately; inventory write-offs require Finance (SAP FI) approval causing multi-day delays before AMOS quantities are corrected

l4_steps.name: Receive and validate parts request from maintenance work order
l4_steps.input: Work order task card, illustrated parts catalogue reference, parts list
l4_steps.output: Validated picking list generated in AMOS; estimated staging time confirmed to technician
l4_steps.kpi: Parts picking initiated within 30 minutes of WO request submission
l4_steps.pain_point: Late parts requests from technicians (defects discovered mid-task) disrupt shop flow; AMOS WO-to-stores interface requires sub-task closure before parts issuance, slowing technician access during time-critical events

l4_steps.name: Kit and stage parts at work centre before task start
l4_steps.input: Validated picking list, bin locations, task start time
l4_steps.output: Kitted parts trolley staged at work centre; all P/Ns and quantities verified
l4_steps.kpi: Kitting accuracy ≥99%; kit staged ≥1 hour before scheduled task start
l4_steps.pain_point: Last-minute P/N substitutions (alternate part approved for use) require a Quality Inspector re-verification before issuance; kitting errors discovered at point-of-use cause unplanned AOG delays averaging 2–4 hours

l4_steps.name: Issue parts to technician and record WO consumption in AMOS
l4_steps.input: Kitted parts, technician badge and signature, work order number
l4_steps.output: Parts issued; WO consumption record updated; removed serviceable/unserviceable parts tagged and returned to stores
l4_steps.kpi: Parts issuance documentation completeness 100%; removed parts tagged within 1 hour of removal
l4_steps.pain_point: Technicians informally borrowing parts without AMOS issuance record causes inventory inaccuracy and traceability failures — a regulatory non-compliance risk under FAR Part 43 and EASA Part 145.A.42

l4_steps.name: Tag and track removed unserviceable rotable in AMOS
l4_steps.input: Removed component, completed work order removal record
l4_steps.output: Unserviceable tag applied; unit status set to U/S in AMOS rotable tracking module with part history appended
l4_steps.kpi: Rotable U/S tagging compliance 100%; AMOS update completed within 4 hours of removal
l4_steps.pain_point: Missing part histories on purchased used rotables from secondary market; AMOS rotable module requires manual re-entry of pre-purchase records from prior operators, with no standardised data exchange format

l4_steps.name: Assess repair viability against BER threshold
l4_steps.input: Unserviceable rotable, OEM Component Maintenance Manual, preliminary repair cost estimate
l4_steps.output: Repair or BER decision documented; repair order raised in AMOS or scrapping order approved
l4_steps.kpi: BER rate ≤8% of annual rotable pool; average repair cost vs. new-unit cost ≤60%
l4_steps.pain_point: OEM shop visit pricing (especially CFM International LEAP engine components) is non-transparent and has risen >25% since 2022 due to supply shortages; BER thresholds require quarterly recalibration to remain accurate

l4_steps.name: Ship core to approved repair agency and track shop visit TAT
l4_steps.input: Raised repair order, serviceable-to-repair shipping documentation, export/import permits
l4_steps.output: Core shipped with AMOS shop visit opened; TAT clock started; interim exchange unit sourced if required
l4_steps.kpi: Repair TAT ≤30 days for avionics LRUs; ≤60 days for engine accessory components
l4_steps.pain_point: Third-party MRO shop visit visibility is limited; AMOS shop visit module does not receive real-time status feeds from external MRO providers — manual status chasing required, with average 10-day response lag inflating fleet-level rotable pool size

l4_steps.name: Receive repaired rotable and return to serviceable stock
l4_steps.input: Repaired unit, MRO shop work order, EASA Form 1 or FAA 8130-3, updated part history
l4_steps.output: Rotable returned to serviceable stock in AMOS; shop visit closed; cost posted to SAP asset record
l4_steps.kpi: Rotable pool availability rate ≥92%; receiving and return-to-stock processing ≤4 hours
l4_steps.pain_point: Repaired units occasionally returned at a different modification standard or with higher-than-quoted cost; configuration mismatch requires re-inspection and potential work-order revision, delaying return to pool by 1–3 days

l4_steps.name: Monitor FAA/EASA AD publication feed
l4_steps.input: FAA ACAS / EASA AD database daily RSS feed
l4_steps.output: New AD log entry with urgency classification
l4_steps.kpi: AD logged within 24 hrs of publication; 100% capture rate
l4_steps.pain_point: Manual monitoring of multiple regulatory feeds (FAA, EASA, TCCA) creates gaps when engineer is on leave; no automated ingestion in legacy CAMP configurations

l4_steps.name: Classify AD urgency — Emergency, Priority, Routine
l4_steps.input: AD text, compliance deadline, subject system ATA chapter
l4_steps.output: AD urgency category assigned; emergency ADs flagged to Accountable Manager within 2 hrs
l4_steps.kpi: Emergency ADs escalated within 2 hrs of receipt; 0 missed emergency ADs
l4_steps.pain_point: FAA Emergency ADs may have 0-day compliance windows that conflict with active aircraft in revenue service, forcing AOG decisions without operational slack

l4_steps.name: Log AD record and open compliance tracking
l4_steps.input: Classified AD from Step 1.2
l4_steps.output: AMOS AD record created with deadline, ATA chapter, and assigned engineer
l4_steps.kpi: AD record created in AMOS within 4 hrs of classification; 100% traceability
l4_steps.pain_point: Duplicate AD entries occur when engineers create records independently in AMOS and CAMP before integration sync runs, causing reconciliation rework

l4_steps.name: Pull aircraft configuration records for AD ATA chapter
l4_steps.input: AD applicability criteria (aircraft type, series, modification status)
l4_steps.output: List of tail numbers with configuration state for affected ATA chapter
l4_steps.kpi: Configuration match completed within 8 hrs; 0 tail numbers missed
l4_steps.pain_point: Config records in CAMP may lag behind actual installed mods if AMOS SB status is not synced in real time — risk of incorrect applicability determination

l4_steps.name: Determine fleet-wide AD applicability
l4_steps.input: Aircraft configuration records, AD applicability logic
l4_steps.output: Applicability determination: list of affected vs not-affected tail numbers
l4_steps.kpi: Applicability determination completed before 50% of compliance window expires
l4_steps.pain_point: Mixed-fleet operators with multiple sub-variants (e.g. 737-700 vs 737-800) frequently have partial applicability — manual cross-check against Boeing TASK data required

l4_steps.name: Evaluate AMOC or interim relief options
l4_steps.input: AD compliance method section; OEM service information; FAA AMOC precedents
l4_steps.output: Decision: accept standard compliance method or initiate AMOC request
l4_steps.kpi: AMOC evaluation completed within 48 hrs of AD receipt for routine ADs
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOC approval from FAA typically takes 30–90 days; if AD compliance window is shorter, airline must comply with original method regardless of cost impact

l4_steps.name: Submit AMOC request to FAA Aircraft Certification Office
l4_steps.input: Engineering justification, test data, equivalent safety analysis
l4_steps.output: AMOC submission reference number; interim relief authorization if granted
l4_steps.kpi: AMOC submitted within 5 business days of decision; FAA acknowledgement within 10 days
l4_steps.pain_point: FAA ACO response times vary by region and workload — AMOC approval is not guaranteed before original compliance deadline, creating dual-track planning burden

l4_steps.name: Create AD compliance work order in AMOS
l4_steps.input: Applicability list, compliance method, deadline from CAMP
l4_steps.output: Work order(s) created in AMOS linked to AD record, with task card reference
l4_steps.kpi: Work orders created ≥14 days before compliance deadline for routine ADs
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS work order creation requires manual linking of AD record to each tail number — no bulk-creation tool for fleet-wide ADs affecting 100+ aircraft

l4_steps.name: Identify and procure required parts and tooling
l4_steps.input: AD task card materials list, current stock levels from AMOS inventory
l4_steps.output: Purchase orders raised; parts reservation against work orders
l4_steps.kpi: Parts confirmed available ≥7 days before scheduled maintenance window; AOG sourcing SLA 4 hrs
l4_steps.pain_point: OEM-only part requirements (no PMA alternatives) for certain ADs create single-source dependency — Boeing / Airbus lead times can exceed AD compliance windows

l4_steps.name: Determine maintenance venue — line vs hangar
l4_steps.input: AD task scope, aircraft access requirements, available maintenance slots
l4_steps.output: Venue decision: line maintenance window or heavy maintenance input
l4_steps.kpi: Venue decision confirmed ≥10 days before compliance deadline
l4_steps.pain_point: Line maintenance slots are constrained by turn-around times (~45 min); structural ADs requiring panel removal force unplanned hangar inputs, displacing scheduled C-check work

l4_steps.name: Schedule and confirm maintenance event
l4_steps.input: Maintenance venue, aircraft rotation schedule from Amadeus SkyWORKS
l4_steps.output: Confirmed maintenance slot; aircraft ground time blocked in ops schedule
l4_steps.kpi: Compliance event scheduled before 75% of deadline window consumed
l4_steps.pain_point: Aircraft rotation optimisation in SkyWORKS does not natively ingest AMOS AD deadlines — manual coordination between MRO planning and network ops required to protect ground time

l4_steps.name: Issue AD task card and brief certifying technicians
l4_steps.input: Approved AD task card, AMM references, special tooling instructions
l4_steps.output: Technician briefing completed; task card issued with required certifications noted
l4_steps.kpi: Task card issued ≥1 hr before planned job start; 0 tasks started without valid authorisation
l4_steps.pain_point: AMM revision cycles can lag behind AD effective dates — technicians may reference superseded procedures if Boeing Toolbox is not updated in sync with AD release

l4_steps.name: Execute AD compliance work per approved maintenance data
l4_steps.input: AD task card, AMM procedures, special tooling
l4_steps.output: Physical work completed; technician sign-off on task card steps
l4_steps.kpi: Zero rework rate due to incorrect procedure; work completed within planned man-hours ±10%
l4_steps.pain_point: Complex structural ADs (e.g. crack inspections under floor panels) can reveal findings not anticipated in original task card, requiring engineering disposition that extends ground time beyond AOG limits

l4_steps.name: Perform independent inspection and buy-back
l4_steps.input: Completed task card, physical inspection of work area
l4_steps.output: QA sign-off; AMOS work order buy-back recorded
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of AD tasks require independent inspection; QA buy-back completed before aircraft release
l4_steps.pain_point: Inspector availability at outstations is limited — line maintenance ADs executed away from main base may require ferry or mobile QA deployment, adding cost and delay

l4_steps.name: Record AD accomplishment in CAMP airworthiness log
l4_steps.input: Signed-off task card, QA buy-back confirmation from AMOS
l4_steps.output: CAMP AD compliance record updated with date accomplished, tail number, and next due date
l4_steps.kpi: CAMP updated within 4 hrs of task completion; 0 gaps in airworthiness record
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS-to-CAMP sync is batch-processed overnight in some configurations — aircraft can technically fly after completion but CAMP still shows AD as open, creating audit exposure

l4_steps.name: Update aircraft technical log and maintenance records
l4_steps.input: Completed buy-back record, AD reference number
l4_steps.output: Aircraft technical log entry; AD compliance endorsement in journey log
l4_steps.kpi: Technical log entry completed before aircraft return to service; 0 releases without AD documentation
l4_steps.pain_point: Regulatory requirements differ by registry (FAA 14 CFR vs EASA Part-M) for how AD compliance must be recorded — dual-registry aircraft require parallel documentation in different formats

l4_steps.name: Assess FAA/EASA regulatory reporting obligation
l4_steps.input: AD text, compliance method used, any deviations or extensions granted
l4_steps.output: Decision: submit formal compliance report or retain on file only
l4_steps.kpi: Compliance reports submitted within 8 calendar days where required by AD text
l4_steps.pain_point: Not all ADs require formal reporting, but ambiguous AD language leads to over-reporting or under-reporting — both carry regulatory penalty risk under FAA Order 8900.1

l4_steps.name: Configure recurring interval alert in CAMP
l4_steps.input: AD next-due parameters (calendar days, flight hours, cycles)
l4_steps.output: Recurring alert configured; next-due dates visible in CAMP due-list dashboard
l4_steps.kpi: Recurring alerts configured within 24 hrs of initial compliance; 0 recurring ADs missed at interval
l4_steps.pain_point: ADs with multi-parameter thresholds (hours AND cycles AND calendar) require compound interval logic that CAMP supports but must be manually validated — error in threshold entry causes silent compliance gap

l4_steps.name: Generate AD due-list report for maintenance planning
l4_steps.input: CAMP due-list data, 30/60/90-day forecast horizon
l4_steps.output: AD due-list report distributed to maintenance planning and operations; items within 30 days flagged
l4_steps.kpi: Due-list report generated weekly; 100% of items due within 30 days actioned with work order
l4_steps.pain_point: CAMP due-list does not automatically interface with AMOS work order scheduling — planners must manually cross-check two systems to confirm no AD falls due during a planned revenue flight

l4_steps.name: Extract technical delay & cancellation events
l4_steps.input: Daily operations data feeds, PIREP submissions, MEL deferrals
l4_steps.output: Reliability event log with ATA chapter coding
l4_steps.kpi: Technical dispatch reliability ≥99.0% (IATA target)
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS data quality degrades at outstations using paper-based PIREP capture; electronic sync lags up to 24 hours, distorting daily reliability figures

l4_steps.name: Compile PIREP and cabin defect report data
l4_steps.input: Pilot reports (PIREPs), cabin defect logs, maintenance findings
l4_steps.output: Consolidated defect database partitioned by ATA chapter
l4_steps.kpi: Repeat defect rate <2% per ATA chapter per month
l4_steps.pain_point: Inconsistent ATA chapter coding across maintenance bases causes mis-classification; repeat defects counted under different chapters, masking true recurrence rates

l4_steps.name: Calculate ATA chapter reliability metrics
l4_steps.input: AMOS defect export, flight operations hours and cycles data
l4_steps.output: ATA chapter reliability scorecard (events per 1,000 flight hours)
l4_steps.kpi: Alert threshold: >3 events / 1,000 flight hours per ATA chapter triggers review
l4_steps.pain_point: Manual data extraction from AMOS via CSV export introduces processing lag of 2–3 days; no real-time API feed from AMOS to BI platform

l4_steps.name: Assess alert threshold breach and escalate
l4_steps.input: ATA chapter reliability scorecard
l4_steps.output: Alert notification issued to MRB, or threshold cleared and monitoring continues
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of threshold breaches assessed within 2 business days of month-end data close
l4_steps.pain_point: Alert threshold logic embedded in legacy spreadsheets not integrated with AMOS or Redshift; threshold parameters updated manually and inconsistently across fleet types

l4_steps.name: Initiate formal failure investigation record
l4_steps.input: Alert notification from MRB, repeat defect flag
l4_steps.output: Investigation record opened in AMOS with case owner assigned
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of Level 1 alert items investigated within 5 business days of alert
l4_steps.pain_point: Insufficient root cause data available when aircraft operated at remote outstations; maintenance findings not captured in AMOS before aircraft repositions

l4_steps.name: Perform MSG-3 logic and FMEA assessment
l4_steps.input: Failure investigation record, OEM Maintenance Planning Document (MPD)
l4_steps.output: FMEA worksheet with failure mode, cause, and effect documented
l4_steps.kpi: FMEA completed for 100% of Level 1 alert items within investigation SLA
l4_steps.pain_point: Boeing Toolbox concurrent-user licence constraints limit simultaneous FMEA sessions; engineers queue for access during peak investigation periods, extending cycle time

l4_steps.name: Classify failure consequence category
l4_steps.input: FMEA worksheet, MPD task data, airworthiness directive index
l4_steps.output: Failure consequence classification: Safety / Operational / Economic / Hidden
l4_steps.kpi: 100% classification accuracy validated by MRB at monthly review
l4_steps.pain_point: Safety consequences misclassified as operational when CAMP airworthiness data is stale due to deferred AD entry; classification errors trigger rework and regulatory exposure

l4_steps.name: Identify and document corrective task recommendation
l4_steps.input: Failure consequence classification, OEM service bulletin index
l4_steps.output: Task change recommendation record with justification and urgency rating
l4_steps.kpi: Recommendation issued within 10 business days of alert escalation
l4_steps.pain_point: OEM (Boeing/Airbus) response SLA for MPD revision guidance averages 45 days, creating a backlog of open recommendations awaiting OEM concurrence before implementation

l4_steps.name: Evaluate existing MPD task applicability
l4_steps.input: Task change recommendation, current approved MPD tasks
l4_steps.output: Task gap analysis identifying intervals to extend, reduce, or replace
l4_steps.kpi: Task revision scope defined within 5 business days of recommendation receipt
l4_steps.pain_point: Mixed 737-700/800/MAX fleet requires parallel MPD analysis tracks; task applicability differs by line number and engine variant, increasing analysis effort by 30–40%

l4_steps.name: Develop revised maintenance task intervals
l4_steps.input: Task gap analysis, reliability trend data, Weibull statistical model output
l4_steps.output: Draft task card revision with updated intervals (FH / FC / calendar)
l4_steps.kpi: Interval extension justified at ≥95% statistical confidence using Weibull analysis
l4_steps.pain_point: Small fleet sample size for 737 MAX subtype (<50 aircraft in some configurations) limits Weibull confidence; task intervals set conservatively, missing potential cost optimisation

l4_steps.name: Assess regulatory change approval requirement
l4_steps.input: Draft task card revision, FAR Part 121.370 compliance matrix
l4_steps.output: Regulatory assessment memo classifying change as self-approval or FSDO submission
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of safety-consequence task changes submitted for FAA/EASA regulatory review
l4_steps.pain_point: Ambiguity in FAR 121.370 on what constitutes a 'significant' maintenance program change requires legal review for borderline cases, adding 5–10 days to the cycle

l4_steps.name: Issue Engineering Order or Maintenance Program Amendment
l4_steps.input: Approved task revision, regulatory assessment memo
l4_steps.output: Engineering Order (EO) or Maintenance Program Amendment (MPA) document
l4_steps.kpi: Engineering Order issued within 15 business days of task approval
l4_steps.pain_point: Concurrent EO backlog regularly exceeds 60 open items; engineering resource constraint delays issuance and causes task cards to remain at superseded intervals in production

l4_steps.name: Submit MPA to FAA FSDO or EASA for approval
l4_steps.input: Maintenance Program Amendment with supporting FMEA and reliability data
l4_steps.output: Regulatory submission package with acknowledgement reference number
l4_steps.kpi: FAA approval turnaround ≤90 days for non-safety items per FAR 121.370
l4_steps.pain_point: FAA FSDO staffing shortages in 2024–2025 causing MPA approval delays beyond 120 days for complex amendments; aircraft continue operating on superseded intervals during review

l4_steps.name: Update approved task cards in AMOS
l4_steps.input: Regulatory approval letter or self-approval sign-off, approved MPA
l4_steps.output: Updated task cards activated in AMOS with new intervals and applicability
l4_steps.kpi: 100% task card accuracy post-update verified by QA within 48 hours of activation
l4_steps.pain_point: Manual task card entry in AMOS prone to interval transcription errors (confusing FH vs FC vs calendar values); errors not caught until next scheduled QA audit cycle

l4_steps.name: Validate task card update accuracy via QA audit
l4_steps.input: Updated AMOS task cards, approved MPA source document
l4_steps.output: QA sign-off record or discrepancy report requiring correction
l4_steps.kpi: Zero task card interval discrepancies at post-update audit; 100% of failed audits remediated within 5 days
l4_steps.pain_point: QA audit sampling rate of 10% for low-risk task revisions may miss low-frequency task card errors on infrequently performed tasks until first work-order execution

l4_steps.name: Train maintenance technicians on revised tasks
l4_steps.input: Approved revised task cards, training needs analysis
l4_steps.output: Training completion records with competency sign-off per technician
l4_steps.kpi: 100% technician training completion within 30 days of task implementation
l4_steps.pain_point: SAP SuccessFactors LMS is not integrated with the AMOS task library; training content must be manually synced, leading to version mismatches between LMS materials and live task cards

l4_steps.name: Generate monthly reliability performance report
l4_steps.input: AMOS reliability data export, flight operations performance data
l4_steps.output: Monthly Reliability Report (MRR) with ATA trend charts and open action items
l4_steps.kpi: Report published within 5 business days of month-end data close
l4_steps.pain_point: Manual consolidation of AMOS export and ops data in spreadsheets creates version control risk; no automated pipeline from AMOS to Tableau, requiring 2–3 days of analyst effort per cycle

l4_steps.name: Present findings to Maintenance Review Board
l4_steps.input: Monthly Reliability Report, open investigation items
l4_steps.output: MRB minutes with closed actions and new action items assigned
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of open MRB action items tracked to closure within agreed timescales; MRB held monthly
l4_steps.pain_point: MRB meeting cadence slips during heavy maintenance check periods; unresolved reliability actions go untracked for up to 60 days, breaching IATA Maintenance Review Board guidelines

l4_steps.name: Assess corrective action effectiveness and close investigation
l4_steps.input: MRB minutes, post-change reliability trend data (90-day lookback)
l4_steps.output: Investigation closure record or re-escalation trigger for repeat failure
l4_steps.kpi: Recurrence rate <5% within 90 days of corrective action implementation
l4_steps.pain_point: Corrective action effectiveness undermined when task changes are not adopted uniformly across all maintenance bases; partial implementation creates split-fleet reliability data that masks recurrence

l4_steps.name: Capture work order completion data in MRO system
l4_steps.input: Completed maintenance task card or work order
l4_steps.output: Closed work order record with technician stamp, part numbers, and man-hours
l4_steps.kpi: Work order closure within 2 hours of task completion; >98% same-shift closure rate
l4_steps.pain_point: Paper-based job cards still used at some line stations — manual re-keying into AMOS introduces transcription errors and delays record closure past the shift boundary

l4_steps.name: Ingest aircraft technical logbook entries
l4_steps.input: Aircraft Technical Log (ATL) — paper or Electronic Technical Log (ETL) feed
l4_steps.output: Digitised logbook entry linked to flight sector and aircraft tail number
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of ATL entries ingested before next departure; ETL integration uptime ≥99.5%
l4_steps.pain_point: ETL interfaces to PSS (Amadeus Altéa) are non-standardised across fleet sub-types; legacy B737-700 may lack ETL hardware, requiring manual paper log reconciliation

l4_steps.name: Validate record completeness against work order schema
l4_steps.input: Ingested work order and logbook entry
l4_steps.output: Completeness check result — pass or list of missing mandatory fields
l4_steps.kpi: Record completeness rate ≥99.5%; incomplete records resolved within 4 hours
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS mandatory-field validation rules vary by maintenance type (line vs. heavy); misconfigured validation profiles cause false-pass records that fail FAA audit spot-checks

l4_steps.name: Cross-reference task against approved AMM/SRM data
l4_steps.input: Closed work order with task card reference
l4_steps.output: Confirmation that executed task matches approved maintenance data revision
l4_steps.kpi: Zero maintenance releases citing a superseded AMM revision; 100% AMM revision currency per Boeing Service Letter cycle
l4_steps.pain_point: Boeing Toolbox AMM revision pushes can lag up to 72 hours behind FAA-approval date; tasks executed on interim revisions may require retroactive re-documentation, increasing rework cost

l4_steps.name: Verify certifying technician licence and authorisation
l4_steps.input: Technician employee ID extracted from work order sign-off
l4_steps.output: Authorisation check result — licence type, rating, and currency status
l4_steps.kpi: Zero maintenance releases by technicians with expired or out-of-scope ratings; authorisation check automated for 100% of closures
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS authorisation matrix must be kept synchronised with FAA A&P licence renewals and airline-specific OJT records; manual update lag creates windows where expired ratings are not flagged

l4_steps.name: Confirm maintenance release and CRS sign-off
l4_steps.input: Verified work order, authorisation check pass, logbook entry
l4_steps.output: Certificate of Release to Service (CRS) or Maintenance Release Statement recorded in AMOS
l4_steps.kpi: CRS issued within 30 minutes of final inspection; 100% of CRS statements traceable to FAR Part 43 / EASA Part-145 signatory
l4_steps.pain_point: Dual-registry aircraft (operating under both FAA and EASA authority) require CRS language compliant with both regulations; AMOS templates are not always jurisdiction-aware, requiring manual text override

l4_steps.name: Update component life-tracking and next-due dates
l4_steps.input: Closed and certified work order with part removals, installations, and time since new (TSN) data
l4_steps.output: Updated component life record showing revised TSN, cycles since new (CSN), and next maintenance due date
l4_steps.kpi: Component record updated within 8 hours of part installation; life-limit threshold accuracy ±0 flight hours/cycles
l4_steps.pain_point: CAMP synchronisation with AMOS relies on nightly batch feeds; intraday part swaps on critical life-limited parts (LLPs) may not appear in CAMP until next morning, creating a brief compliance exposure window

l4_steps.name: Link AD/SB compliance closure record to aircraft serial
l4_steps.input: AD or Service Bulletin number, effectivity, compliance method, and accomplishment date
l4_steps.output: AD compliance entry linked to tail number and fleet record in CAMP
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of applicable ADs reflected in CAMP within 24 hours of task closure; zero open ADs past compliance deadline
l4_steps.pain_point: FAA AD effectivity determination for mixed-variant fleets (737-700/800/MAX 8) is complex; incorrect variant mapping in CAMP can result in ADs being erroneously marked not-applicable, triggering FAA enforcement action

l4_steps.name: Identify overdue or near-threshold compliance items
l4_steps.input: CAMP automated compliance forecast report run daily
l4_steps.output: Prioritised exception list of ADs, LLP limits, and scheduled tasks within 30-day or 100-FH threshold
l4_steps.kpi: Zero items entering the overdue state; 100% of near-threshold items actioned ≥7 days before due date
l4_steps.pain_point: High-frequency short-haul operations (4–6 sector days) can erode compliance buffers faster than weekly planning cycles anticipate; CAMP threshold alerts must be tuned to fleet utilisation intensity to avoid false urgency fatigue

l4_steps.name: Escalate critical airworthiness findings to MCC and Planning
l4_steps.input: Exception list from CAMP with overdue or critical near-threshold items
l4_steps.output: Work order raised in AMOS; maintenance slot requested from MCC; aircraft grounding risk flagged if threshold cannot be met in-service
l4_steps.kpi: MCC notified within 2 hours of threshold breach identification; grounding avoided in ≥95% of escalations through proactive slot allocation
l4_steps.pain_point: MCC operational priority (avoiding flight cancellations) conflicts with airworthiness deadline compliance; without a formal escalation SLA in AMOS, airworthiness items can be deferred repeatedly until a hard grounding is unavoidable

l4_steps.name: Archive work orders per FAA retention schedule
l4_steps.input: Certified and closed work orders exported from AMOS
l4_steps.output: Immutable PDF/A records stored in versioned S3 bucket with metadata tags (tail, date, task reference)
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of closed work orders archived within 24 hours; retention period ≥24 months per FAR Part 121.380 for routine tasks, ≥life of aircraft for major repairs
l4_steps.pain_point: FAR Part 121.380 retention tiers (24-month vs. life-of-aircraft) require automated classification at point of archival; miscategorisation of major repairs as routine tasks has resulted in premature record purges discovered only during aircraft sale due diligence

l4_steps.name: Generate aircraft technical status summary report
l4_steps.input: CAMP compliance data, AMOS work order history, AWS S3 archive index
l4_steps.output: Aircraft Technical Status Report (ATSR) per tail: open deferrals, AD status, LLP remaining life, next check due
l4_steps.kpi: ATSR published weekly for all active tails; zero data discrepancies between ATSR and AMOS/CAMP source systems
l4_steps.pain_point: Tableau dashboards pull from AMOS and CAMP via separate API connectors with different refresh cadences; stale data in one source can make the ATSR appear current while masking an overdue item

l4_steps.name: Validate archived record format for regulatory compliance
l4_steps.input: Archived PDF/A records sampled from S3 for format and metadata audit
l4_steps.output: Validation report confirming PDF/A-1b compliance, metadata completeness, and tamper-evident hash integrity
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of sampled records pass PDF/A validation; zero records with missing mandatory metadata fields; hash verification failure rate 0%
l4_steps.pain_point: PDF/A conversion from AMOS native format occasionally strips embedded digital signatures required by FAA AC 120-78B for electronic records; silent conversion failures are only detected during authority audit

l4_steps.name: Compile records package for FAA/authority audit
l4_steps.input: FAA audit notice specifying scope (tail numbers, date range, AD references)
l4_steps.output: Structured audit evidence package: certified work orders, CRS statements, AD compliance records, technician authorisation records
l4_steps.kpi: Audit package delivered within 5 business days of FAA request; zero findings of missing required records in formal audit
l4_steps.pain_point: Cross-system evidence assembly (AMOS + CAMP + AWS S3 + Boeing Toolbox) is manual; no single orchestration tool exists to compile a complete audit package automatically, creating significant labour cost and risk of omissions under tight FAA timelines

l4_steps.name: Respond to AD compliance queries from airworthiness authority
l4_steps.input: FAA/authority query specifying AD number, effectivity date, and fleet scope
l4_steps.output: Formal compliance response citing accomplishment dates, methods of compliance, and tail-by-tail status exported from CAMP
l4_steps.kpi: AD compliance query response within 10 business days; 100% of responses supported by primary source documentation traceable to original work order
l4_steps.pain_point: CAMP AD compliance reports are formatted for internal use; exporting in FAA-specified formats (e.g., 8130-3 data elements) requires manual reformatting that introduces transcription risk and delays formal response

l4_steps.name: Submit airworthiness certificate renewal documentation
l4_steps.system: FAA DragonWave / FAA PTRS (Programme Tracking & Reporting Subsystem)
l4_steps.input: Compiled ATSR, AD compliance summary, major repair/alteration records, current maintenance programme approval
l4_steps.output: Airworthiness Certificate renewal package submitted to FAA FSDO; certificate issued or discrepancy list returned
l4_steps.kpi: Certificate renewal submitted ≥30 days before expiry; zero aircraft operated with lapsed airworthiness certificate; discrepancy resolution within 15 business days
l4_steps.pain_point: FAA FSDO processing times are variable and outside airline control; late submission driven by internal records gaps can result in aircraft AOG during the renewal window, incurring significant revenue loss and customer disruption

l4_steps.name: Receive AOG defect notification
l4_steps.input: Pilot-raised defect entry via ETL or ACARS message from flight deck
l4_steps.output: AOG defect record opened in MRO system with timestamp and station
l4_steps.kpi: Defect receipt-to-acknowledgement < 5 minutes
l4_steps.pain_point: ETL systems at outstations may lack real-time ACARS integration, forcing phone-based defect relay that delays MCC awareness by 10–20 min

l4_steps.name: Assess defect against MEL / CDL
l4_steps.input: Defect description, aircraft type/registration, departure time
l4_steps.output: MEL/CDL applicability decision: relief granted or AOG confirmed
l4_steps.kpi: MEL assessment completed < 15 minutes of defect receipt
l4_steps.pain_point: MEL revision cycles lag OEM amendments by up to 30 days if airline OpSpec approval is delayed, leaving engineers working from printed fallback copies

l4_steps.name: Apply MEL relief and replan dispatch
l4_steps.system: AMOS by Swiss AviationSoftware + Amadeus Altéa Operations
l4_steps.input: MEL relief decision, any associated placard or operational restriction
l4_steps.output: MEL deferred defect item raised, aircraft re-dispatched with restriction noted in flight release
l4_steps.kpi: MEL-cleared aircraft released within 30 minutes of defect; on-time departure recovery ≥ 85%
l4_steps.pain_point: Altéa Operations and AMOS operate as separate systems; MEL deferrals must be manually mirrored to flight release, creating risk of dispatching crew without restriction awareness

l4_steps.name: Classify AOG severity and estimate RTA
l4_steps.system: AMOS by Swiss AviationSoftware (AOG workflow module)
l4_steps.input: Confirmed AOG defect record, affected flight schedule, station capability matrix
l4_steps.output: AOG severity code (AOG-1 / AOG-2 / AOG-3), Return-to-Airworthy (RTA) estimate, passenger impact assessment
l4_steps.kpi: AOG classification completed < 10 minutes of MEL decision; RTA estimate accuracy ± 1 hour for 80% of events
l4_steps.pain_point: RTA estimates at remote outstations with limited history are often optimistic; underestimation cascades into multiple re-protection waves, amplifying passenger disruption costs

l4_steps.name: Alert station maintenance and mobilise team
l4_steps.system: SITA ACARS / Airline Crew Communication Platform
l4_steps.input: AOG classification, station engineer roster, aircraft bay location
l4_steps.output: Station LAME and supporting technicians dispatched to aircraft with tooling kit
l4_steps.kpi: First engineer on aircraft within 20 minutes of AOG declaration at main bases; 45 minutes at outstations
l4_steps.pain_point: Outstations with single contracted line maintenance providers may have engineers committed to concurrent turnarounds, delaying AOG response beyond contractual SLA by 15–30 minutes

l4_steps.name: Check local parts availability for likely defect
l4_steps.input: Suspected defect ATA chapter, aircraft type, station warehouse stock snapshot
l4_steps.output: Parts availability confirmation or shortage flag sent to MCC within 10 minutes
l4_steps.kpi: Station first-time fill rate ≥ 60% for top-20 AOG consumable part numbers
l4_steps.pain_point: Inventory data in AMOS at outstations can be up to 4 hours stale if warehouse staff have not confirmed physical receipts; MCC dispatches engineers expecting parts that are not present

l4_steps.name: Perform initial inspection and fault isolation
l4_steps.system: Jeppesen FliteDeck / OEM Fault Isolation Manual (FIM)
l4_steps.input: Defect description, aircraft built-in test equipment (BITE) readout, fault codes
l4_steps.output: Confirmed ATA chapter fault code, probable cause, and required corrective action identified
l4_steps.kpi: Fault isolated within 45 minutes for 90% of LRU-level defects
l4_steps.pain_point: BITE data on older aircraft variants (e.g. A320 CFM56 legacy FDR) requires cross-referencing paper FIM charts; digital FIM integration with AMOS is not universal across fleet types

l4_steps.name: Access AMM / IPC repair procedures
l4_steps.system: Boeing Toolbox / Airbus AiRTHM / Trax (document integration)
l4_steps.input: Confirmed ATA fault code and part number from fault isolation
l4_steps.output: Approved AMM task card retrieved and printed/displayed for repair execution
l4_steps.kpi: Correct AMM revision accessible within 5 minutes; zero deferred task cards performed on superseded revisions
l4_steps.pain_point: AMM revision synchronisation between OEM publication dates and airline-approved libraries lags by 15–45 days; engineers at outstations may access a local cached version that pre-dates a critical service bulletin

l4_steps.name: Escalate to OEM engineering support if unresolved
l4_steps.system: Boeing AeroExchange / Airbus AiRTHM OEM AOG Desk portal
l4_steps.input: Unresolved fault after AMM fault isolation steps exhausted, BITE logs, photos
l4_steps.output: OEM engineering instruction (TEO/TEM) or disposition issued within agreed SLA
l4_steps.kpi: OEM first response < 2 hours (AOG priority); disposition received < 4 hours for 85% of escalations
l4_steps.pain_point: OEM AOG support SLAs differ by aircraft type and contract tier; low-utilisation carriers on basic support contracts wait up to 8 hours for dispositions, extending AOG duration into multi-day events

l4_steps.name: Activate AOG desk for emergency parts sourcing
l4_steps.system: AMOS (Purchasing / AOG Order module) + ILS Partsbase
l4_steps.input: Required part number(s), quantity, urgency (AOG priority), station and RTA
l4_steps.output: AOG purchase order raised; parts located at OEM, distributor, or pool inventory
l4_steps.kpi: AOG PO raised < 15 minutes of parts shortage confirmation; vendor acknowledgement < 1 hour
l4_steps.pain_point: ILS Partsbase and AMOS purchasing are not natively integrated; coordinators toggle between platforms increasing error risk in part number / revision level transcription

l4_steps.name: Coordinate cross-fleet loan or borrow with partner airline
l4_steps.system: AMOS (Loan/Borrow module) + direct AOG desk contact
l4_steps.input: Unmet AOG PO, part number, adjacent airline AOG desk contacts at affected station
l4_steps.output: Loan agreement confirmed, part released from partner fleet, paperwork (Form 1 / 8130-3) transmitted
l4_steps.kpi: Loan agreement confirmed < 2 hours of initial AOG desk activation; traceability documents received before part installation
l4_steps.pain_point: Loan/borrow transactions require bilateral airworthiness approval (EASA Form 1 or FAA 8130-3); delays in receiving signed release documentation from partner engineers hold up installation even when part is physically available

l4_steps.name: Arrange priority shipment to AOG station
l4_steps.system: AMOS + DHL / FedEx AOG courier portal
l4_steps.input: Parts sourced and ready for dispatch, RTA, nearest airport with scheduled freight service
l4_steps.output: AOG courier shipment booked, AWB number logged in AMOS, ETA confirmed to station
